title: FAQ
heading: Clear answers,
intro: Grouped by what people usually want to know first. Tap any question to open it — nothing here is timed or tracked, so come back as often as you like.

what.question: What is cervical screening?
what.answer: A simple test that checks cervical cells for HPV, the virus that can lead to changes over time. Most results are normal.

why.question: Why is it important?
why.answer: Screening can find HPV before it causes cell changes. Finding changes early means they can be followed up before they develop into cervical cancer.

who.question: Who should be screened, and from what age?
who.answer: In Australia, cervical screening is recommended every five years for people aged 25 to 74 who have a cervix, including people who have had the HPV vaccine.

howOften.question: How often do I need to go?
howOften.answer: Most people need a test every five years. Your healthcare provider may suggest a different plan based on your result or health history.

test.question: What actually happens during the test?
test.answer: A small sample is collected from the cervix by a trained healthcare professional. The test usually takes a few minutes, and you can ask to pause at any time.

femaleClinician.question: Can I ask for a female doctor or nurse?
femaleClinician.answer: Yes. You can request a female healthcare provider when booking. You can also bring a support person or ask for an interpreter.

cost.question: Does screening cost anything?
cost.answer: The cost can depend on where you go and your circumstances. Ask the clinic about any fees before making an appointment.

selfCollect.question: Can I collect my own sample?
selfCollect.answer: Self-collection may be available for eligible people. Ask your healthcare provider whether it is an option for you.

whatIs.question: What is HPV?
whatIs.answer: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common group of viruses. Most HPV infections clear naturally, but some types can cause cell changes that may eventually lead to cervical cancer.

howSpread.question: How do people get HPV?
howSpread.answer: HPV spreads mainly through intimate skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity, including vaginal, anal and oral sex. It can spread even when neither person has symptoms.

prevention.question: How can I prevent HPV?
prevention.answer: HPV vaccination helps protect against the types most likely to cause cervical cancer. Using condoms can reduce the risk but cannot prevent all HPV infections. Cervical screening is also important because it can detect HPV and help identify people who need follow-up.

positiveResult.question: What should I do if I test positive for HPV?
positiveResult.answer: A positive HPV result does not mean you have cervical cancer. HPV is common and often clears naturally. Follow the advice in your screening results and attend any recommended follow-up tests or appointments with your healthcare professional.

results.heading: Understanding your cervical screening results
results.intro: Your result helps determine whether you need another screening test or further follow-up. Here is what each result category means.

lowRisk.title: Low risk (HPV not detected)
lowRisk.description: No high-risk HPV was found in your sample. Your chance of developing cervical cell changes that need treatment in the next five years is very low. You will generally be invited to have another cervical screening test in five years.

intermediateRisk.title: Intermediate risk
intermediateRisk.description: HPV types 16 and 18, which carry the highest risk, were not detected, but another high-risk HPV type was found. Your sample has also been checked for abnormal cell changes, and there are either no changes or only minor changes. You will generally be asked to return in 12 months for a follow-up HPV test, as your body will often clear the infection over time.

higherRisk.title: Higher risk
higherRisk.description: This may mean HPV types 16 or 18 were detected, high-grade cervical cell changes were found, or another high-risk HPV infection has persisted. Further follow-up is important to assess your risk and determine whether treatment is needed. A higher-risk result does not necessarily mean you have cervical cancer.

unsatisfactory.title: Unsatisfactory result
unsatisfactory.description: Your sample could not be examined adequately. This may happen if there were too few cells or insufficient sample material for the required tests. It does not mean that HPV was detected or that an abnormality was found. You should repeat the test at the time recommended by your healthcare professional.
